title: Kinematics
summary: A particle moving along a straight line has a [[displacement|displacement]] $s$, a [[velocity|velocity]] $v$ and an [[acceleration|acceleration]] $a$. Differentiate to go from $s$ to $v$ to $a$, and integrate to go back. [[speed|Speed]] and [[distance-travelled|distance travelled]] ignore direction, so they both use $\lvert v\rvert$.

goals.text: Differentiate [[displacement|displacement]] to get velocity and acceleration, and find when a particle is at rest.
Find [[speed|speed]] as the size of the velocity, and use signs to tell the direction and whether the particle is speeding up.
Integrate velocity to find displacement, from a known position or as $\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.
Find the total [[distance-travelled|distance travelled]] as $\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \lvert v(t)\rvert\,\mathrm{d}t$: by splitting at $v = 0$ on Paper 1, or with your GDC on Paper 2.

synonyms: particle moving in a straight line
when is the particle at rest
integral of absolute value of velocity

before.hint: Use the chain rule: differentiate the sine, then multiply by the derivative of $3t$.
before.explain: $\sin$ differentiates to $\cos$, and the inside $3t$ gives a factor of $3$. So the derivative is $5 \times 3\cos(3t) = 15\cos(3t)$. Revise it in {{lesson:5.6}}.

before.hint: Integrate to get $f(t)$ with a $+\,C$, then put $t = 1$ and $f(1) = 5$ in to find $C$.
before.explain: $f(t) = 3t^{2} - 2t + C$, and $f(1) = 3 - 2 + C = 5$ gives $C = 4$. Revise it in {{lesson:5.5}}.

before.hint: Find an antiderivative $F(t)$, then work out $F(2) - F(0)$.
before.explain: An antiderivative is $F(t) = t^{3} + t$, so the integral is $F(2) - F(0) = 10 - 0 = 10$. Revise it in {{lesson:5.5}}.

blocks.text: Picture a bead sliding along a straight wire. Fix a point O on the wire and choose one direction as positive. The bead's [[displacement|displacement]] $s$ is its position measured from O.

blocks.statement: The displacement $s$ of a particle at time $t$ is its position relative to a fixed point O on its line of motion, positive on one side of O and negative on the other.
blocks.plain: It tells you where the particle is, not how far it has moved.

blocks.text: The rate at which $s$ changes is the [[velocity|velocity]] $v$. The rate at which $v$ changes is the [[acceleration|acceleration]] $a$. These are rates of change, as in {{lesson:5.1}}.
The acceleration line is in the formula booklet; learn the velocity line. Units follow the rates: with $s$ in metres and $t$ in seconds, $v$ is in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $a$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
A particle is at rest at an instant when $v = 0$. "Initial" means at $t = 0$.

blocks.question: A particle moves along a straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point O after $t$ seconds is $s = 2t^{3} - 15t^{2} + 24t$ metres, for $t \ge 0$. Find expressions for $v$ and $a$. Hence find the times when the particle is at rest.
steps: Differentiate $s$ for the velocity: $v = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t} = 6t^{2} - 30t + 24$.
Differentiate again for the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 12t - 30$.
Factorise: $(t - 1)(t - 4) = 0$, so $t = 1$ or $t = 4$. Both satisfy $t \ge 0$, so keep both.

blocks.prompt: A particle has displacement $s = t^{3} - 4t^{2} + 5$ metres at time $t$ seconds. Find its velocity, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, at $t = 3$.
blocks.explain: $v = 3t^{2} - 8t$, so $v(3) = 27 - 24 = 3$. The value $-4$ is $s(3)$, the position, and $10$ is $a(3)$, from differentiating twice.

blocks.question: A particle moves on a straight line. Its displacement is $s = 6\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)$ metres at time $t$ seconds, for $0 \le t \le 6$. Find the acceleration of the particle the first time it is at rest.
steps: Differentiate with the chain rule. The inside, $\frac{\pi t}{3}$, has derivative $\frac{\pi}{3}$. So $v = 6 \times \frac{\pi}{3}\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right) = 2\pi\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)$.
Differentiate again: $a = 2\pi \times \frac{\pi}{3} \times \left(-\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)\right) = -\frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)$.
At rest means $v = 0$, so $\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right) = 0$. At $t = 0$ the cosine is $1$, so the first solution is $\frac{\pi t}{3} = \frac{\pi}{2}$, which gives $t = \frac{3}{2}$.
Substitute $t = \frac{3}{2}$ into $a$. Since $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1$, $a = -\frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}$.
Don't solve $a = 0$ here: that gives $t = 0$, $3$ or $6$, the wrong times.

blocks.prompt: A particle has displacement $s = t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 15t$ metres at time $t$ seconds, $t \ge 0$. Find its acceleration, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$, at the later of the two times when it is at rest.
blocks.hint: Solve $v = 0$ for the two times. Then differentiate $v$ and substitute the larger time.
blocks.explain: $v = 3t^{2} - 18t + 15 = 3(t - 1)(t - 5)$, so the particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 5$. Then $a = 6t - 18$, and $a(5) = 12$.

blocks.text: "Write down the initial velocity" needs only $v(0)$, with no further working. Give units, such as $\text{m s}^{-1}$, whenever the question uses them.

The sign of $v$ gives the direction. When $v > 0$, $s$ is increasing, so the particle moves in the positive direction. When $v < 0$ it moves in the negative direction. This is {{lesson:5.2}} again: a positive derivative means an increasing function.

blocks.statement: The speed of a particle is the magnitude of its velocity: $\text{speed} = \lvert v\rvert$.
blocks.plain: Speed is how fast the particle goes, with no direction attached, so it is never negative.

blocks.text: A car reversing at $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ has [[velocity|velocity]] $-3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ if forwards is positive. Its [[speed|speed]] is $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

blocks.question: A particle has velocity $v = t^{2} - 6t + 5$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $t \ge 0$. Find its speed at $t = 2$, and state which way it is moving.
steps: Substitute $t = 2$: $v = 4 - 12 + 5 = -3$.
The velocity is negative, so at $t = 2$ the particle is moving in the negative direction.
Speed is the size of the velocity: $\lvert -3\rvert = 3$.

blocks.statement: A particle changes direction at a time when $v$ changes sign. $v = 0$ on its own is not enough.
blocks.why: Direction is the sign of $v$. If $v$ touches $0$ but keeps its sign, as $v = (t - 2)^{2}$ does at $t = 2$, the particle pauses and carries on the same way.

blocks.statement: A particle is speeding up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign. It is slowing down when they have opposite signs.
blocks.why: Speed is $\lvert v\rvert$. When $v$ and $a$ are both negative, $v$ gets more negative, so its size grows. When their signs differ, $v$ moves towards $0$.

blocks.question: The particle above has velocity $v = t^{2} - 6t + 5$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, for $t \ge 0$. Find the intervals of time when it is speeding up.
steps: Factorise: $v = (t - 1)(t - 5)$. So $v < 0$ for $1 < t < 5$, and $v > 0$ for $0 \le t < 1$ and $t > 5$.
Differentiate: $a = 2t - 6$. So $a < 0$ for $t < 3$ and $a > 0$ for $t > 3$.
Compare signs between the key times $1$, $3$ and $5$. The signs match on $1 < t < 3$ (both negative) and for $t > 5$ (both positive).
On $0 \le t < 1$ and $3 < t < 5$ the signs differ, so the particle is slowing down there.

blocks.text: "Moving in the positive direction" means $v > 0$. It does not mean $v$ is increasing, which is $a > 0$. Read the graph of $v$ for where it is above the axis, not where it rises.

blocks.prompt: A particle has velocity $v = 3\cos(2t)$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds. Use your calculator, in radians, to find its speed at $t = 1$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Work out $v(1)$ first. Speed is its size, so drop any minus sign.
blocks.explain: $v(1) = 3\cos 2 = -1.2484\ldots$, so the speed is $1.2484\ldots \approx 1.25\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Degree mode gives $2.998\ldots$, which is wrong.

blocks.prompt: A particle has velocity $v = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 9t$, for $t \ge 0$. What happens at $t = 3$?
blocks.hint: Factorise $v$. Then look at the sign of $v$ just before and just after $t = 3$.

options.text: It is at rest for an instant, then keeps moving in the positive direction
It is at rest for an instant, then moves in the negative direction
It is not at rest: it is moving in the positive direction

blocks.explain: $v = t(t - 3)^{2}$, which is $0$ at $t = 3$ but positive on both sides. The particle stops for an instant, then carries on the same way.

blocks.text: At HL you also describe motion with a vector line: the direction vector is the velocity and its magnitude is the speed.

Now go the other way, from [[velocity|velocity]] back to [[displacement|displacement]]. Differentiating $s$ gives $v$, so $s$ is an [[antiderivative|antiderivative]] of $v$. Integrating $v$ gives $s$, up to a constant $C$.

To find $C$ you need one known position, such as $s = 3$ when $t = 1$. This is the [[boundary-condition|boundary condition]] method from {{lesson:5.5}}. The same works one level up: $v = \int a\,\mathrm{d}t$, with $C$ fixed by a known velocity.

blocks.question: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v = 6t^{2} - 4t$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. When $t = 1$, its displacement from O is $3$ m. Find an expression for its displacement $s(t)$.
steps: Integrate the velocity: $s = \int (6t^{2} - 4t)\,\mathrm{d}t = 2t^{3} - 2t^{2} + C$.
Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2t^{3} - 2t^{2} + 3\right) = 6t^{2} - 4t$, which is $v$.

blocks.prompt: A particle has acceleration $a = 6t$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Its initial velocity is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Find its velocity, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, at $t = 2$.
blocks.hint: Integrate $a$ to get $v$ with a $+\,C$. "Initial" means $t = 0$, which gives $C$.

blocks.text: Often you don't need $s$ itself, only how much the position changes between two times $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$. That change is $s(t_{2}) - s(t_{1})$. By {{lesson:5.5}}, it is the [[definite|definite integral]] of $v$.
This is in the formula booklet. It gives where the particle is at $t_{2}$ compared with where it was at $t_{1}$. You don't need the starting position, because the $C$ cancels when you subtract.

blocks.question: A particle has velocity $v = 8 - 2t$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds. Find its displacement from $t = 1$ to $t = 6$.
steps: Write the integral first: $\text{displacement} = \int_{1}^{6} (8 - 2t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.
An antiderivative of $8 - 2t$ is $8t - t^{2}$.
Substitute the limits and subtract: $(48 - 36) - (8 - 1) = 12 - 7 = 5$.
So at $t = 6$ the particle is $5$ m on the positive side of where it was at $t = 1$.

blocks.prompt: A particle has velocity $v = 3t^{2} - 6t$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Find its displacement, in metres, from $t = 0$ to $t = 3$.
blocks.hint: Integrate $v$ from $0$ to $3$. Don't split it: displacement keeps the signs.
blocks.explain: An antiderivative is $t^{3} - 3t^{2}$, so the displacement is $(27 - 27) - 0 = 0$. $8$ is the distance travelled, $-4$ stops at $t = 2$, and $9$ is $v(3)$.

blocks.text: Treating "the displacement from $t_{1}$ to $t_{2}$" as the position $s(t_{2})$. They are equal only when the particle is at O at time $t_{1}$.
[[distance-travelled|Distance travelled]] is what a car's mileage counter records: every metre counts, forwards or backwards. Unlike [[displacement|displacement]], it is never negative.

blocks.statement: The total distance travelled between $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ is the total length of path the particle covers in that time, in either direction.
blocks.plain: It adds up every metre moved, including the way back.

blocks.alt: Velocity against time for v equals 8 minus 2t. Between t equals 1 and 4 the line is above the t-axis and the shaded triangle has area 9. Between t equals 4 and 6 it is below the axis and the shaded triangle has area 4.
blocks.caption: For $v = 8 - 2t$ from $t = 1$ to $t = 6$: the area above the axis is $9$ and the area below is $4$.

blocks.text: Go back to the [[velocity|velocity]] $v = 8 - 2t$. From $t = 1$ to $t = 4$, $v > 0$ and the particle moves $9$ m forwards. From $t = 4$ to $t = 6$, $v < 0$ and it moves $4$ m back. The integral of $v$ gives $9 - 4 = 5$, but the distance travelled is $9 + 4 = 13$.
This is in the booklet too. Taking $\lvert v\rvert$ makes every backward stretch positive, so nothing cancels. On Paper 1, by hand, split the time wherever $v = 0$:
1. Solve $v = 0$ to find the times inside the interval where the particle may turn.
2. Integrate $v$ over each piece between those times.
3. Add the sizes of the pieces, ignoring their signs.
Using $\int v\,\mathrm{d}t$ for distance. Backward motion is then subtracted, as the $5$ instead of $13$ above shows. Integrate $\lvert v\rvert$, or split at $v = 0$.

blocks.question: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v = t^{2} - 4t + 3$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0 \le t \le 4$. Find its displacement over the 4 seconds, then the total distance it travels.
steps: Factorise: $v = (t - 1)(t - 3)$, so $v = 0$ at $t = 1$ and $t = 3$. Between them $v < 0$; outside them $v > 0$.
Displacement: $\int_{0}^{4} v\,\mathrm{d}t = F(4) - F(0) = \frac{4}{3}$ m.
The three pieces: $F(1) - F(0) = \frac{4}{3}$, then $F(3) - F(1) = -\frac{4}{3}$, then $F(4) - F(3) = \frac{4}{3}$.
Add the sizes: $\frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = 4$, three times the displacement, because the particle went back and then forwards again.

blocks.prompt: A particle has velocity $v = 2t - 4$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0 \le t \le 5$. Find the total distance, in metres, that it travels.
blocks.hint: Find when $v = 0$. Integrate each side of that time separately, then add the sizes.
blocks.explain: $v = 0$ at $t = 2$. With antiderivative $t^{2} - 4t$, the pieces are $-4$ and $9$, so the distance is $4 + 9 = 13$. $5$ is the displacement; $9$ leaves out the first piece.

blocks.text: On Paper 2, write the integral of $\lvert v\rvert$ down and let the GDC evaluate it. No splitting is needed.

blocks.question: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity is $v(t) = 4\cos(1.2t) + 0.5t$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $0 \le t \le 5$. Use your calculator to find the displacement from $t = 0$ to $t = 5$, and the total distance travelled in that time. Give your answers to 3 s.f.
steps: Set the GDC to radians, since the angle $1.2t$ is in radians.
Displacement: write down $\int_{0}^{5} \left(4\cos(1.2t) + 0.5t\right)\mathrm{d}t$. The GDC gives $5.3186\ldots$, so the displacement is $5.32$ m.
Graph $v$: it crosses the axis at $t = 1.4621\ldots$ and $t = 3.5444\ldots$, so the particle turns twice and the distance is more than $5.32$ m.
Distance: write down $\int_{0}^{5} \left\lvert 4\cos(1.2t) + 0.5t\right\rvert\mathrm{d}t$. The GDC gives $12.636\ldots$, which rounds to $12.6$ m.

blocks.prompt: A particle has velocity $v = 2\sin(2t)$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Use your calculator to find the total distance it travels from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.explain: $\int_{0}^{2} \lvert 2\sin(2t)\rvert\,\mathrm{d}t = 2.3463\ldots \approx 2.35$. Without the modulus you get $1.65$, the displacement: $v$ turns negative after $t = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

blocks.text: For "find the total distance travelled" on Paper 2, write the integral of $\lvert v\rvert$ with its limits before the value. That line shows your method and can earn a mark even if the value is wrong.
At rest: $v = 0$. Changes direction: $v$ changes sign. Speed $= \lvert v\rvert$.
Speeding up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign; slowing down when they differ.
Distance on Paper 1: split at each $v = 0$, integrate each piece, add the sizes.

mistakes: Using $\int v\,\mathrm{d}t$ for distance, or giving the final displacement as the distance. A particle that goes $9$ m out and $4$ m back has displacement $5$ m but has travelled $13$ m.
Mixing up $v = 0$ and $a = 0$. The particle is at rest when $v = 0$; where $a = 0$, the velocity may be at a maximum or minimum.
Reading "moving in the positive direction" as "velocity increasing". The first is $v > 0$; the second is $a > 0$.
Leaving the GDC in degree mode for a velocity with $\sin$ or $\cos$. Set radians first.
Keeping a time outside the domain. If $t \ge 0$, reject a negative root of $v = 0$.
examTips: "Justify" that a particle changes direction: show that $v$ changes sign, for example with values of $v$ either side. Showing $v = 0$ alone is not enough.

"Find the total distance travelled": on Paper 2, write $\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \lvert v(t)\rvert\,\mathrm{d}t$ with the numbers in, then the GDC value. On Paper 1, show the times when $v = 0$ and each piece.
If a later part uses an earlier answer, such as a time when $v = 0$, a wrong value used correctly can still earn follow-through (FT) marks.
Give 3 s.f. unless told otherwise, with units such as $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Carry full GDC values and round only at the end.
